content: Key characteristics of deceased individuals that are relevant to HIV programming, such as whether the person belonged to a specific HIV risk group, are often not recorded. This lack of data complicates the calculation of differential mortality rates among population groups. However, in cases where it is legally and ethically permissible to link individual data across various service delivery points, it may be possible to cross-reference the number of AIDS-related deaths recorded in vital statistics systems with facility records of patient deaths. Several countries, including Brazil and South Africa, have successfully linked data from diverse sources such as censuses, vital statistics, and HIV-specific databases. To encourage governments to invest in civil registration and vital statistics (CRVS) systems, the WHO Health Metrics Network published a document in 2012 titled The Case for Investment in Civil Registration and Vital Statistics Systems. This document outlines the necessity, scope, and cost of a functioning CRVS system. Additionally, WHO and UNAIDS have recently issued guidance on measuring HIV mortality. Health information systems are designed to collect data from various sources in a standardized format, enabling analysis and sharing with stakeholders to support program planning and decision-making. Organizing data within a comprehensive system is critical for assessing the health sector cascade. This involves collecting and reporting data on HIV diagnoses, case reporting, and patient monitoring, as well as implementing best practices for data management, including the use of unique identifiers, data security, confidentiality, interoperability, and data flow. Standardized individual patient records serve multiple purposes, supporting quality services at individual, facility, district, and national levels. As clinical management tools, these records help healthcare providers deliver appropriate services to individuals. As monitoring and evaluation (M&E) tools, they facilitate the transcription of key data elements into monitoring systems for use at various levels. Patient care information is recorded in individual patient records (e.g., HIV care cards or patient files), with key information transferred into longitudinal registers for easier follow-up and reporting. These records should be securely stored to protect patient confidentiality and be easily retrievable for patient care. Structured clinical records improve patient care by prompting comprehensive assessments, enabling quick reviews of patient management across visits, and ensuring the completion of all data elements. However, challenges include ensuring timely and accurate completion of records by busy healthcare providers. Training, supervision, and user-friendly layouts can help address these issues. Data collection should focus on elements directly related to patient care or key national reporting indicators. Paper registers and reporting forms are commonly used in health information systems to compile data for multiple patients. These registers, often longitudinal, track individual patients over time and can be used to follow cohorts based on defined starting points, such as ART initiation. Reporting forms should clearly define the data elements to be entered and be designed to minimize the burden on staff. Electronic data systems offer significant advantages over paper-based systems, including the ability to track patient-level data over time, aggregate data more efficiently, and enable detailed analysis. These systems can link patient data across facilities using unique identifiers, integrate with other software (e.g., laboratory and pharmacy systems), and provide timely, detailed reports. However, electronic systems require dedicated staff for data entry and maintenance, as well as ongoing technological support. Offline systems are simpler and less costly to implement, while online systems offer greater functionality but require more infrastructure and resources. When transitioning from paper-based to electronic systems, it is important to avoid overburdening data collection points with excessive variables. Electronic systems are more expensive and require capacity-building, equipment, and ongoing support. Online systems, in particular, demand significant investment in networking and infrastructure. Despite these challenges, many countries are moving toward electronic reporting systems to improve data quality and service delivery. The DHIS2 software is a widely used tool for collecting, validating, analyzing, and presenting aggregate health data. It is modular, web-based, and built on open-source frameworks, allowing users to design information systems without programming expertise. DHIS2 supports the collection and management of transactional, case-based data and enables longitudinal tracking of patient records. It also offers advanced data visualization features, such as GIS, charts, and dashboards. By improving data quality and enabling real-time validation, DHIS2 enhances the accuracy and utility of health information systems. The choice of system should be guided by the available resources, infrastructure, and the specific needs of the health sector.
